Senses.Explanation: The Accord of Difference and Sameness is the title of Shitou Xiqian’s verse, identified as a composed work, quoted by its opening and closing lines, and discussed by later masters. The title combines participation or joining , sameness , and accord or tally . In the Chan corpus it is the proper name of Shitou Xiqian's verse. The Transmission of the Lamp says that Shitou wrote it, calls its language deep, and prints the work under his name. Its opening says that the mind of the great Indian immortal is intimately transmitted east and west ; its closing tells the person investigating the mystery to meet the source on hearing words and not waste the daylight . Fayan Wenyi later invokes the title in hall discourse, calls it a piece of wording, and quotes its opening. The Joint Essentials of the Lamps connects Shitou's composition with his reading that the sage has no self and nothing is not himself . Zen bends the phrase into a lineage-specific bibliographic name: these records use it not for a general agreement but for Shitou's transmitted Chan poem and for quotations from that poem.

Senses.Explanation: To visit and question a lineage figure is not merely to ask for information. In these records the headword names the student's entry into a face-to-face encounter: Tanran and Huairang arrive and immediately ask the meaning of the ancestor's coming from the west, while Juzhi answers every visiting student's inquiry by raising one finger. Biographical uses also measure a student's career by whom he consulted, or pointedly say that he asked nobody. The word therefore marks public, answerable contact in which a student exposes his question.

Senses.Explanation: To join, attend, or report to the communal hall. Biographical records use the expression for formal admission: people seeking to join the hall might wait for months, while a favored visitor is admitted that same day; Wuzu orders Yuanwu to join the hall immediately, after which Yuanwu enters the attendants' quarters. In encounter records the imperative 'go to the hall' regularly closes or dismisses an exchange. Wuju says it after striking two visitors, and Wenshu Siye shouts it to a former butcher, who then goes down to the hall. In commentary on the rhinoceros-fan case, an unnamed monk tells the entire assembly to go to the hall, and Yuanwu explicitly says that the unnamed monk has seized the authority of the host. The institutional and imperative uses share the same hall-directed action.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 529 matches in 137 files. The imperative 'go to the hall' accounts for 349 matches in 99 files, including seven matches in six files that address the whole assembly. The nominal form 'those who seek or attend the hall' occurs four times in four files; 'ordered him immediately to join the hall' occurs ten times in ten files, and 'then went down to the hall' occurs nineteen times in sixteen. These forms distinguish this institutional use of 'join' from other senses of the first graph elsewhere in Chan vocabulary.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names sustained investigation of Chan rather than merely learning information about it. Gaofeng Yuanmiao says that investigating Chan requires an iron person whose mind is decided on taking it up, calls the great matter of life and death its crucial point, and compares its aim of awakening with livelihood's aim of wealth. Zhongfeng Mingben criticizes people who speak of investigating Chan only with their mouths and turn encounter records into conversation material. Xueguan Zhiyin insists on determined effort rather than merely staring toward the school’s signboard. Dahui Zonggao retrospectively calls his own years before breakthrough investigation of Chan; Konggu Daocheng joins it to strenuous personal effort. An unnamed lay questioner asks Yongjue Yuanxian where investigating Chan gains force. Together these uses denote committed inquiry directed toward resolving the great matter, while warning that verbal cleverness does not constitute that inquiry.

Senses.Explanation: To investigate the particular word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out from a recorded exchange. Frozen-corpus concordance: 195 exact hits in 81 storage files representing 81 independent works. Poshan Haiming identifies what remains unresolved in a scripture or public case as one's personally investigated saying. Zhongfeng Mingben supplies the actual question, 'Why did Zhaozhou say the word no?', and directs the listener to investigate that wording and raise great doubt. Zhanran Yuancheng says to investigate one's own selected saying in earnest, while Ruibai Mingxue says to place it before one and keep it continually in mind. Other witnesses explicitly police the action: Zhuanyu Heng criticizes seeking the wording in books and other people's mouths and asks whether those who perform it differ from those who do not; Zongbao Daodu says earlier patriarchs did not teach people to investigate sayings and presents the instruction as a later response to proliferating calculations; Gumei You says not to speculate over public cases or search in scriptures. Zen bends recorded public speech into the selected object of investigation, while the same records challenge where the wording is sought, what the action is taken to accomplish, and whether it should be reified.

Senses.Explanation: A visit to a named instructor or assembly in order to ask questions and request instruction. It occurs 243 times in 121 allowlisted texts and includes both institutional attendance and the encounter itself. Zhicheng leaves Shenxiu, travels to Shaoyang, and "joins the assembly to visit and inquire" (隨眾參請); Shuangfeng Gu's biography says that at Shishuang he merely followed the assembly and "no longer visited and inquired" (更不參請). The monastic regulations place "traveling from place to place to visit and inquire" (遊方參請) under a heading that lists departure from one's teacher, seeking a respected elder, requesting lodging, first reporting to the guest office, and next registering at the hall office. Huanyuan Fuyu "bent his knees to visit and inquire" (屈膝參請), after which Lingyin Tai addressed his understanding. Tianning's monastic and lay followers visited and inquired morning and evening while Huqiu Shaolong answered them without weariness (晨夕參請，師與唱酬無倦). The recorded actions are visits, institutional participation, questions, and responses in Chinese Chan texts.
Senses.Note: Productive constructions mark the same range: "join the assembly to visit and inquire" (隨眾參請, 27 occurrences), "enter the room to visit and inquire" (入室參請, 2), "travel from place to place to visit and inquire" (遊方參請, 6), and headings for "circumstances of visiting and inquiry" (參請因緣, 2). Fayan can ask what scripture someone reads "apart from visiting and inquiry" (於參請外), placing it among the ordinary activities of a visitor's life. The Blue Cliff Record contrasts a superintendent's not having "visited and inquired or entered the room" (不曾參請入室) with Fayan subsequently asking why he does not come enter the room. The overlap between travel, residence in an assembly, and direct exchange is native to the term, so these are kept as deployments of one sense.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the lineage seal transmitted and applied to mind
Senses.Explanation: A lineage seal said to be transmitted from teacher to heir and applied to mind: the records preserve stamp grammar rather than a physical object. The term occurs 1,374 times in 280 allowed texts. Chuming Baoyin says the ancestral mind-seal is neither long nor short, square nor round, inside nor outside, nor in between (祖師心印，非長非短，非方非圓，非內非外，亦非中間). Jingjie Shoumi says it has no trace or shape and remains distinct and uninterrupted through the ages (祖師心印，無痕無狀。歷劫分明，未嘗間斷). Fengxue Yanzhao compares it to the mechanism of an iron ox: 'going, it seals and holds; staying, it seals and breaks' (去即印住。住即印破). Shishuang Chuyuan says one seal imprints empty space, water, and mud (一印印空。一印印水。一印印泥). Huangbo Xiyun says Bodhidharma 'secretly transmitted the mind-seal, imprinting your original mind; mind imprints the teaching, and the teaching imprints mind' (密傳心印，印你本心。以心印法，以法印心). Sengna says the ancestral mind-seal does not consist exclusively in harsh conduct (祖師心印非專苦行), while Weishan Huaixiu says the mind-seal of buddhas and ancestors is known only through confirmation (佛祖心印，唯證乃知). These are the corpus's formal, material, and transmission predicates; they do not turn the seal into a literal implement.
Senses.Note: Required definition formulas found no single prose gloss of the bare compound, but several direct shape-negations and seal-mechanism explanations. 'Ancestral mind-seal' (祖師心印) occurs 368 times in 162 texts, while 'mind-seal of buddhas and ancestors' occurs 23 times in 17. Proper-name uses belong to the separate personal-title sense below.

A later address quotes "it cannot be known by wisdom or recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off, the place of mental activity extinguished," then answers with a deliberate counter-formulation: "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off, mental activity is not extinguished" (心行不滅). Zhongfeng also reports an interpreter's equation: "cut off thought, then the place of mental activity is extinguished" (絕慮則心行處滅), before contesting that line of equation in the following passage. The entry therefore records the fixed pair, explicit parallel, question, and counter-witness rather than equating the phrase with blankness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 切莫將身心別處雜用。饒你掉臂，也是祖師西來意，脚尖頭也踢出一尊古佛來。不如無事好。上堂，舉黃龍三關話，師曰：黃龍老漢頭匾，所以說漳泉福建話逼真。謾得天下人過，謾漳泉福建人不過。上堂：以手指左邊者是香爐，指右邊者是華瓶。

Senses.Explanation: Huanglong Huinan's three barriers (黃龍三關) are: 'Where is your birth-origin?', 'How does my hand resemble the Buddha's hand?', and 'How does my foot resemble a donkey's foot?' Lamp records preserve the questions together, say that Huanglong raised them for more than thirty years, and report that he neither approved nor rejected answers. Huanglong explains that one already through a barrier walks straight on rather than asking the gatekeeper for approval. Later masters raise, versify, contrast, and criticize the named set; those are deployments of the inherited case, not additional barriers.
